articles.title: Virginia Dems cast doubt on prosecution of colleague after embracing criminal allegations against Trump
articles.summary: Virginia Democrats who called allegations and investigations into Trump justified now stress the presumption of innocence after one of their own faces federal charges.
articles.body: Virginia Democrats who previously defended investigations and allegations against Donald Trump are urging restraint now that federal prosecutors have charged one of their own. The shift is evident across the party's top ranks following the indictment of Virginia Senate President Pro Tempore L. Louise Lucas. Lieutenant Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, who rejected Republican claims that Trump was being selectively prosecuted after his 2023 classified-documents indictment, is now stressing Lucas' "constitutional presumption of innocence" and arguing Lucas "is fully entitled to legal due process." Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones, who said last year that Trump tried to "incite a riot" and "overturn an election," says the allegations against Lucas must be tested through a legal process "free from political interference or bias." Rep. Bobby Scott, D-Va., likewise joined Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine in declaring that "those charged with crime are innocent until proven guilty" and questioning the Justice Department's motivations — years after Scott said during Trump's first impeachment that "the facts are uncontested," called his conduct a "gross abuse of presidential power" and declared that "no one is above the law." Trump was later acquitted by the Senate. POWERFUL DEM’S JABS AT TRUMP COME BACK TO HAUNT HER AFTER OFFICE RAIDED BY FBI: ‘AGED WELL’ Gov. Abigail Spanberger, meanwhile, is stressing Lucas' presumption of innocence after calling congressional defenses of Trump's handling of classified documents "deeply detrimental to our national security" days after his 2023 indictment in a case that was ultimately dismissed without a trial. Lucas, who also chairs the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee, was indicted alongside six others in what federal prosecutors allege was a years-long criminal enterprise involving marijuana distribution, money laundering, bribery and fraud. She has denied wrongdoing, and an indictment does not establish guilt. The investigation that ultimately produced the charges began during the Biden administration, according to multiple reports. The contrasting rhetoric extends beyond individual officeholders. The Democratic Party of Virginia (DPVA) declared Trump had been "rightfully indicted" and that "no one is above the law" immediately after a Manhattan grand jury indicted him in March 2023 — more than a year before a jury heard the case. The party had also criticized Republican claims that federal law enforcement was being politically "weaponized" against Trump during the classified-documents investigation. Lucas currently serves as a DPVA vice chair. TOP SPANBERGER ALLY TARGETED IN FBI CORRUPTION PROBE HAS LONG HISTORY OF CONTROVERSY Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., was the only Democrat contacted by Fox News Digital who responded to questions about the contrast between his past rhetoric about Trump and his current rhetoric about Lucas, rejecting the suggestion that his positions were inconsistent while accusing federal law enforcement of politically timing Lucas' arrest. "It doesn't matter if you're a Democrat or Republican, the American people deserve answers and accountability from everyone," Subramanyam told Fox News Digital. Subramanyam called the charges against Lucas "serious," adding that "she should face justice if they are true," while alleging that "the DOJ and FBI timed this arrest for two weeks before the election for political reasons." "Trump has a pattern of targeting political opponents and weaponizing the DOJ, and he has spent his second presidency covering up the Epstein files," Subramanyam said. "It took Congress forcing the administration's hand to even get a fraction of the full files released." VIRGINIA DEMS SPLIT ON DOJ PROBE OF SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF GIVING 'SWEETHEART DEALS' TO ILLEGAL ALIENS The federal investigation that produced Lucas' indictment, however, predates Trump's second administration. The Washington Post, CBS News and The Associated Press reported after federal searches in May, citing anonymous sources familiar with the investigation, that the probe began during the Biden administration. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche reiterated that the investigation began years ago and rejected allegations of political retaliation. "We don't do political paybacks," Blanche said. Federal prosecutors allege Lucas led a criminal enterprise involving relatives and associates that distributed marijuana and laundered proceeds while she used her political position to protect the operation and influence legislation that could financially benefit it. The indictment alleges Lucas and her co-defendants were involved in distributing at least 100 kilograms of marijuana, while FBI Director Kash Patel said the alleged scheme generated roughly $4.5 million. "I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them." "I will not be bullied," she added. "And I will not back down."

articles.title: California must respond to DOJ's emergency request over ballots mailed to alleged noncitizens, court rules
articles.summary: The DOJ says roughly 20,000 noncitizens received mail-in ballots in California and is demanding the state sequester those votes before they are processed.
articles.body: A federal appeals court ordered California to respond by noon Saturday to the Trump administration's emergency request involving roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots sent to people the Justice Department suspects are noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit issued the order late Friday after the DOJ filed an emergency request earlier in the day seeking a ruling by Saturday. The Justice Department sought emergency relief from the appeals court after U.S. District Judge David Carter did not rule by a deadline previously requested by the department. The DOJ is asking California election officials to set aside ballots associated with individuals on its list while their eligibility is reviewed, rather than allowing the ballots to be processed alongside other votes. DOJ GIVES CALIFORNIA 48 HOURS TO REVIEW LIST OF POSSIBLE NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS In its emergency filing, the DOJ emphasized the urgency of its request. "This is an emergency," the filing, submitted by Attorney General Todd Blanche and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, stated. "Every minute of processing that occurs without segregating the ballots of suspected non-eligible voters causes untraceable disenfranchisement and dilution of the votes of United States citizens," the filing continued. Despite the Ninth Circuit's order, a hearing before Judge Carter remains scheduled for Tuesday, according to Fox News' Matt Finn. It remains unclear whether the appeals court will rule before that hearing. BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO Essayli previously told Fox News Digital that federal investigators have evidence showing the 20,000 individuals received mail-in ballots in October. His office sued California last week seeking a court order to prevent ballots returned by those individuals from being counted. "We're not asking California to take any drastic steps other than to sequester the ballots from the suspected noncitizens," Essayli said in an interview Wednesday. "We believe it's at a minimum of 20,000. That's the floor." Essayli also clashed with California Gov. Gavin Newsom on social media this week over the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting. Essayli accused California of allowing noncitizens onto its voter rolls because of what he described as inadequate citizenship verification procedures, while Newsom defended the integrity of the state's elections and maintained that California was following the law. ‘RAW MATERIAL FOR ELECTION FRAUD’: EXPERT FLAGS VOTER-ROLL PROBLEMS FAR BEYOND ONE STATE California election officials have rejected the Justice Department's demands. In court filings, they argued that county election offices lack both the authority and access to federal records needed to verify voters' citizenship status. They also said separating ballots associated with people on the DOJ's list would be impossible in cases where the ballots have already been processed. California officials say that once a mail-in ballot's signature has been verified, the ballot is separated from its identifying envelope and processed with other ballots. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP According to court records, officials have already processed 331,000 ballots in Los Angeles County alone. Friday's escalation comes after Essayli's office initially filed the suit Oct. 15, roughly two weeks after California began mailing ballots. Fox News Digital's James Cirrone contributed to this report.

articles.title: GREGG JARRETT: Ilhan Omar could face indictment, denaturalization and deportation
articles.summary: Minn. Rep. Ilhan Omar faces a federal probe into alleged identity fraud, marriage fraud, and false statements that could possibly lead to denaturalization and deportation.
articles.body: Lies, particularly spectacular ones, inevitably crumble over time when subject to scrutiny. A case in point is Rep. Ilhan Omar. She is suspected of hatching a series of epic deceptions about her identity, lineage, birthdate, marriage, and citizenship status. An investigation by federal authorities culminated in a recent search of her home that was authorized by a judicial warrant. On the same day, multiple other search warrants were executed in different locations, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullen. DNA evidence was reportedly obtained. Her computer devices, document files, cell phones, and notebooks were seized. More than a dozen grand jury subpoenas were allegedly served on Omar’s family, including her sister. ILHAN OMAR IS NOT THE MINNESOTA CONGRESSWOMAN’S 'REAL NAME': SOURCES Omar has not been indicted. Yet. She denies all wrongdoing, asserting that she is a victim of a politically driven vendetta by the Trump administration. Let’s examine that. The warrant on Omar’s home was approved by a Democratic judge in the District of Columbia, a venue with a long and conspicuous hostility toward Trump and anyone in his orbit. It is reasonable to conclude, therefore, that the feds must have presented substantial incriminating evidence to justify the signed order, especially against a sitting member of Congress from the judge’s own party and just weeks before an important election. Yes, the threshold of probable cause for a warrant is lower than the trial standard of "beyond a reasonable doubt." But the judge’s decision was not nothing. He was persuaded by compelling evidence of criminality. Apparently, he spent hours examining the merits of the warrant application. Action was taken lest evidence be destroyed. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS While the specifics of the investigation remain unclear, we are acquainted with the general parameters. They pose troubling questions. Is Ilhan Omar the person she purports to be? Was her immigration to the U.S. secured through falsehoods? Was her citizenship obtained validly or through lies? Are the rumors true that Omar engaged in a sham marriage to her brother in a scheme to obtain immigration benefits for him? FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE As always, the answers depend on the reliability of the evidence collected and the credibility of witnesses. articles.title: Why a blue wave might miss Minnesota’s Senate race
articles.summary: Political headwinds are blowing in Democrats’ favor nationally, with high gas prices and President Trump’s record-low approval rating creating a difficult midterm environment for Republicans. But in Minnesota’s open Senate race to replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D), Democrats are facing an unexpectedly competitive race. Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) holds a slim lead over…
articles.body:
Political headwinds are blowing in Democrats’ favor nationally, with high gas prices and President Trump’s record-low approval rating creating a difficult midterm environment for Republicans.

But in Minnesota’s open Senate race to replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D), Democrats are facing an unexpectedly competitive race.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) holds a slim lead over former sports reporter Michele Tafoya (R) that’s only narrowed , according to limited public polls ahead of Election Day.

Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report recently shifted the race in the GOP’s favor — from “likely” to “lean” Democrat, citing Flanagan’s underperformance in polling compared to Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D), who is running for governor, a statewide fraud scandal and Republicans notching a strong recruit in Tafoya.

And while Tafoya has an uphill battle in a state that has not elected a Republican to the Senate in nearly 25 years, Flanagan’s biggest political vulnerability stems from her nearly eight years serving under Gov. Tim Walz (D).

“This is one of the races that could be so close we might have a recount,” said longtime Minnesota political analyst Blois Olson, who called Flanagan’s proximity to the fraud scandal “a little bit like ankle weights around her campaign.”

The sprawling welfare fraud scandal that has engulfed the Walz administration has become a major pain point for the progressive candidate.

Walz abandoned his reelection bid for a third term in January as the allegations of up to billions of dollars in fraud within Minnesota social service programs attracted criticism both in Minnesota and nationally. Flanagan, Walz’s running mate in 2018 and 2022, is one of few in the Walz administration facing voters this November.

Republicans are hoping voters’ frustrations over the administration’s handling of fraud and the anti-incumbency wave will extend to the lieutenant governor, with no incumbent running for governor or the Senate.

“Peggy Flanagan allowed fraudsters to plunder billions in taxpayer dollars on her watch, and now she’s facing questions about her own inflated academic record,” Bernadette Breslin, a spokeswoman for the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, said in a statement to The Hill. “Minnesotans aren’t buying the excuses Flanagan is selling, and they’re counting on Michele Tafoya to protect their hard-earned tax dollars.”

Tafoya has made the fraud scandal a central part of her campaign, arguing that Flanagan and the rest of the Walz administration should be held accountable for failures that occurred during her tenure.

“Why has no one been fired?” Tafoya said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal . “The only real consequence we’ve seen is that Tim Walz was convinced to step out of his third term gubernatorial race because there was no way he was going to survive this. But Peggy Flanagan’s asking for a promotion.”

Even aspects of Flanagan’s personal background have been more heavily scrutinized in recent weeks. The Wall Street Journal initially reported earlier this week that the Minnesota progressive had not been a member of the Phi Beta Kappa honors society, with the campaign saying that while Flanagan was nominated, she couldn’t afford the membership fee.

However, the honor society later provided The Hill and other news outlets a statement, which confirmed she had been a member. The campaign told The Hill that the newspaper’s questions over her status with the honor society prompted internal confusion, and they weren’t able to offer confirmation of her membership to the Journal in time for publication.

Flanagan’s campaign pushed back on Tafoya over her handling of the statewide fraud scandal, pointing to the distinction between the governor’s and the lieutenant governor’s responsibilities.

A campaign official said Walz oversees state agencies and programs, while Flanagan’s statutory duties are more limited.

The official acknowledged that more should have been done sooner to address the fraud and that the issue was personal for Flanagan, who relied on Medicaid and Section 8 housing at one point in her life.

The Tafoya campaign did not respond to a request for comment from The Hill.

While the widespread fraud scandal has put Flanagan on the defensive, Tafoya also faces a political liability of her own with Trump’s souring popularity in the state and as the price of items like gas and fertilizer have shot up amid an ongoing war with Iran and a tariff war with Canada.

Uproar over Trump’s federal immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, which led to two U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)-involved shootings, has also complicated Tafoya’s efforts to balance her appeal to both Trump’s steady voter base and independent voters who may be more reluctant to support Republicans in statewide elections.

“The fraud thing — that it hangs over the state of Minnesota — certainly is a bit of a drag for Democrats, but at the same time, the Trump administration, I still think, is a bigger drag on the Republicans,” said former Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DLF) Party chair Mike Erlandson.

Tafoya has taken steps in recent weeks to distance herself from the president.

When asked for a reaction to the president’s endorsement at a Monday night debate, Tafoya said, “There is one endorsement that I care about and that is the one that happens on Nov. 3.”

Tafoya criticized the president over the war in Iran during a recent interview with CBS News , saying “the war in Iran has gone on longer than I think people were ready for and we’re suffering at the gas pump.” Earlier this year, the GOP candidate caught flak for suggesting people should make “one less trip to Starbucks” to save on gas, and that the country should be supporting its military while it’s engaged in the conflict.

In a midterm environment that historically serves as a referendum on the party in power, Democrats have made no secret about tying Tafoya to Trump and the national GOP.

A Flanagan campaign official pointed out that Tafoya “earned” her endorsement from Trump by being loyal to him and his policies, noting her support of him in the past.

“In the last month before the election, she wants to try and walk away from all the positions that she’s been holding for years,” the spokesperson told The Hill, arguing that her recent stepping away from the president was inconsistent with her earlier positions.

And national Democrats feel confident about their odds of keeping the state within the fold give their recent track record. They point out, too, that national Republican groups have spent little money on the contest, which they say is an acknowledgement from within the GOP that the race isn’t in play.

“Republicans haven’t won a Minnesota Senate race in more than 20 years and that losing streak will continue in 2026 when Minnesotans elect Democrat Peggy Flanagan,” Maddy McDaniel, a spokeswoman for the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm, who dubbed Tafoya as “a Trump loyalist and a wealthy Republican activist.”

Some Republicans say the anti-incumbent energy could hit the parties either way.

“We have also a large number of undecideds in these polls, and I think they’re truly undecided because I think that it depends on the day,” said former GOP Minnesota Senate Majority Leader Amy Frederiksen, who’s not working on the Senate race.

“They go and fill up their tank, and they’re ticked off about Iran and tariffs,” she said, adding that “the next news story they see is … another 10 million or another 15 million stolen, and nobody did anything about it,” referring to the statewide fraud scandal.

articles.title: Early voting surges in battleground states as Democrats outpace GOP gains
articles.summary: Early voting is surging in several key battleground states, giving Democrats hope that their strength in midterm polling could translate into a turnout advantage in November. In North Carolina, more than 1.2 million early ballots have been accepted, a 37 percent increase from the same point leading up to the 2022 midterms, according to an…
articles.body:
Early voting is surging in several key battleground states, giving Democrats hope that their strength in midterm polling could translate into a turnout advantage in November.

In North Carolina, more than 1.2 million early ballots have been accepted, a 37 percent increase from the same point leading up to the 2022 midterms, according to an analysis released Friday by Catawba College political scientist Michael Bitzer.

That growth — which includes both in-person and mail-in ballots — has been driven by a 47 percent increase among registered Democrats and a 60 percent increase in participation among unaffiliated voters. Early voting among Republicans is up 2.6 percent.

Similar patterns are emerging elsewhere, with high turnout especially pronounced in historically Republican-leaning states with competitive Senate races this cycle.

More than 23 million ballots have been accepted nationwide, compared with more than 15 million reported at a similar point ahead of the 2022 midterms. In Kansas, early voting is up roughly 69 percent, while it’s up 41 percent in Maine and 24 percent in Iowa, according to a New York Times analysis of state election records and voter data through Thursday.

Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political science professor who tracks early voting, said Democrats and unaffiliated voters are similarly outpacing Republicans in turnout gains compared to 2022 across states where he has comparable party registration data — including Kansas, Maine, Iowa and Nebraska.

“It’s the same pattern. Democrats and unaffiliateds are engaged. Republicans are not as engaged,” McDonald told The Hill, adding, “And it explains why you might be seeing this shift of the battleground into these red states. Overall, there’s just more engagement among Democrats.”

McDonald cautioned that there is a range of factors that can affect states’ early voting numbers, including changing timelines for when mail-in ballots are sent out.

There are also limits to what early voting data can reveal. Not all states record party registration, and there’s no guarantee that a voter’s party affiliation will match that of the candidate they choose to support.

But McDonald said the early voting patterns give credence to polls showing Democrats in a strong position heading into Election Day.

“The early voting data is just telling me that what we know from the polling data is correct. That yes, the polling is not telling us something wrong. There’s not some big polling miss on the horizon,” McDonald said.

In Texas, Democrats are hoping Senate nominee James Talarico can end the party’s more than three-decade drought in statewide elections. But Texas does not register voters by party, making it harder to determine whether Democrats’ strength in polling is translating into an early turnout advantage.

Decision Desk HQ’s modeling suggests a narrower partisan gap than in some other states. Of the 2.06 million ballots cast in person or returned by mail as of Thursday, an estimated 44.3 percent came from Democratic voters and 43.7 percent came from Republicans. Among Hispanic early voters, the model estimates Democrats outnumber Republicans by roughly 2.5 to 1.

Democrats are also pointing to strong participation in Travis County, a Democratic stronghold that includes Austin.

More than 158,000 in-person ballots were cast during the first four days of early voting, up roughly 61 percent from the same point in 2022 and 19 percent from 2018, according to a compilation of state election data provided by the county Democratic Party. The county’s registered electorate has also grown since 2018, so the increase in ballots does not necessarily represent a higher participation rate.

“In Travis County, where Democrats really need to run up the score, we’re beating 2022 and 2018 turnout levels—elections when Beto [O’Rourke] was on the ballot—and pacing towards 2024 turnout,” Luke Warford, chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said in a statement to The Hill.

But higher turnout in Democratic strongholds alone will not be enough for Talarico to win in November, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston.

“Democrats don’t just need high turnout to win statewide. They need urban margins large enough to overcome rural margins, and Republicans’ rural floor has risen since 2018,” Rottinghaus said. “High turnout is necessary for Democrats, but not sufficient.”

He also noted that high turnout this cycle is “not only a Democratic story,” saying there’s a “slight purple tinge to the turnout so far,” and redder, rural areas are “slow out of the gate but catching up.”

In Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is favored to fend off his Republican challenger, voters also do not register by party, “so we can only make guesses about who is turning out to vote based on geography and demographic factors,” said Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at Emory University.

Early voting is slightly higher this year, with approximately 1.5 million ballots cast through Thursday, up from roughly 1.4 million at the same point in 2022, according to the Times analysis.

Gillespie said Democrats likely benefit from elevated turnout among Black voters and among voters living in the metropolitan areas of Atlanta, Athens, Savannah, Macon and Augusta. But she said participation is also strong in traditionally Republican areas, like Cherokee and Forsyth counties.

“Democrats have been trying to make inroads there, so it is not clear whether the people turning out are Democrats or Republicans yet,” she said.

In Virginia, where Democrats are targeting several GOP-held House seats, nearly 930,000 early ballots had been cast through Thursday, roughly 80 percent more than at the same point in 2022, according to the Virginia Public Access Project.

“Early voting in Virginia has been concentrated in congressional districts where Republicans are playing defense, not offense,” University of Mary Washington political scientist Stephen Farnsworth said.

He noted that, although Virginians do not register by party, “polling shows far more interest in voting among Democrats than Republicans.”

Several factors could still influence turnout in the next week. Republicans have time to narrow the participation gap, and GOP voters have historically turned out more heavily on Election Day.

President Trump’s shifting message on mail-in ballots could also affect voter behavior. He has repeatedly attacked and tried to restrict mail voting but has more recently encouraged Republicans to vote early or by mail.

“The big question this year is whether Republicans are more likely to take advantage of early voting now that President Trump has relaxed his rhetoric about why one should only vote on Election Day,” Gillespie said. “If Republicans vote alongside Democrats in early voting, then we may not see Election Day surges in voting in Republican areas that we have seen in the past.”

McDonald, meanwhile, said concerns about mail voting could push some Democrats to vote in person, reducing the likelihood of their ballots being rejected. More than half a million mail ballots were rejected for various reasons in 2024, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission.

“If there are fewer people who are voting by mail, and it’s particularly Democrats, that means that there are going to be fewer Democratic rejected mail ballots,” McDonald said.

“Trump may have inadvertently done a favor to the Democrats by encouraging their voters to vote in person, and we’re seeing that in the in-person early voting.”

articles.title: Minnesota candidate ‘stress tests’ state’s new fraud law — what she found raised major red flags
articles.summary: Heidi Heino says she stress-tested Minnesota's inspector general law against Feeding Our Future and found critical gaps in fraud prevention safeguards.
articles.body: A Minnesota state Senate candidate revealed she found several vulnerabilities in a fraud prevention law signed by Gov. Tim Walz after testing it against the state’s previous fraud scandals to see whether it could have caught them sooner. The measure in question, the Office of the Inspector General law, creates an independent statewide watchdog that oversees inspectors general, investigates alleged fraud across state programs, establishes fraud prevention standards, and improves coordination and data sharing. However, Heidi Heino, the Republican candidate for Minnesota’s 36th Senate District, told Fox News Digital her test against the Feeding Our Future scheme and other past fraud cases found the law lacks extra safeguards when potential risks emerge. "When I stress tested against Feeding Our Future and some of the other fraud schemes that we had in Minnesota, it would have found the fraud eventually, but it's way after the money was already gone and we would still be stuck trying to claw it back," Heino said. MINNESOTA MAN CAPTURED IN SOMALIA AFTER ALLEGEDLY HELPING ORCHESTRATE $250M CHILD NUTRITION FRAUD SCHEME The law was passed as Minnesota faces the fallout from massive fraud schemes involving childcare, autism, housing and disability services. Republicans have blamed leadership and oversight failures, while the Trump administration launched a federal anti-fraud task force led by Vice President JD Vance. Working as a corporate leader whose day job involves underwriting, Heino said she used similar review and auditing practices to test where Minnesota’s fraud safeguards fell short. "Business does a lot with a little," she said. "Government does the opposite. They do a little with a lot of resources." Heino said she used a 2,800% increase in payments to Feeding Our Future from 2020 to 2021 in her test, a jump that should have automatically raised alarm bells and led to further review. The scheme alone allegedly stole $250 million from a federally funded child nutrition program during the COVID-19 pandemic. FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD, OTHER MAJOR SCAMS: 'CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE' "You don't have to be a detective to see that there's some issue there and so to investigate that and check and see if those claims are legitimate, and if they were legitimate, have someone actually sign off on it," she said, adding that filling out extra paperwork may be frustrating but can help prevent fraud in the long run. Heino also argued Feeding Our Future should not have been allowed to address complaints against itself. "We had 30 complaints to the Minnesota Department of Education regarding the fraud and they are mostly overlooked or Feeding Our Future had to go correct itself and that was a huge gap there," she said. She proposed immediately freezing payments, conducting a full review, and triggering an outside audit. "The OIG has good bones, but it needs teeth," she said. Without independent audits, Heino said Minnesota will not be able to uncover fraud-related gaps, saying the additional oversight would save more money than it costs. GOP ACCUSES WALZ ALLIES OF BURYING $52M MEDICAID FRAUD REPORT BEFORE ELECTION "We get a lot of pushback saying this is going to be expensive, but is it?" she said. "It will be less expensive to have an independent audit than it is going to be to have all the fraud and lose taxpayer dollars to fraudulent activities." Those same issues apply to current state programs like Minnesota’s Paid Leave program, according to Heino. "However, we need to rein it in and have more investigation before we start sending out the checks, especially with paid family leave," she said. "They pay out before they have the doctor's note certifying that this is actually true and they have verified it." She acknowledged that the law is a "great first step" toward addressing the problem but said it does not go far enough to protect taxpayers and prevent future fraud. As a mother, grandmother and taxpayer, Heino said she is fed up with how leaders in her home state have handled fraud, adding the problem has gotten so bad that Minnesota has become the "laughing stock of the nation" and people no longer want to say they are from the state anymore. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We need to funnel those resources to the people that actually need them and keep people committing fraud from taking our money and running away with it, buying luxury condos or homes, and then funneling it out of the country," she said. Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office and the Minnesota Department of Education for comment. "We have not slowed down, there is no sense in which the fraud has been stopped in Minnesota," Bill Glahn, a policy fellow at the Center of the American Experiment, told Fox News Digital in August, making the case that the fraud situation in the state has not been properly addressed.
